title: Give a Function the Full Situation
content:
What problem does this solve?
One input is sometimes not enough to describe the work a function must do. A function can declare several parameters so each required piece of information has its own name.

Match from left to right
  def label(name, role):
      return f"{name}: {role}"
  label("Mira", "Scout")
With a normal positional call, Python matches the first argument to the first parameter and the second argument to the second parameter. Order therefore matters.

Use every required input
A parameter should exist because the function needs that information. Hidden tests should change each input so hardcoded or ignored values cannot pass.

Vocabulary after the behavior
A parameter is the name in the function definition. An argument is the value supplied in one call. Positional arguments are matched from left to right.
concepts: Functions can declare several required parameters
Positional arguments match parameters from left to right
Argument order can change the result
Every required parameter should contribute to the function's behavior

examples.title: Two required inputs
examples.explanation: The first argument becomes a and the second becomes b.

examples.title: Order matters
examples.code:
def label(first, second):
    return f"{first}-{second}"
print(label("A", "B"))
print(label("B", "A"))
examples.explanation: Swapping positional arguments swaps which parameter receives each value.

common_mistakes: Passing arguments in the wrong order
Adding parameters but then hardcoding one of their values in the body
Confusing parameter names in the definition with argument values at the call site
Assuming Python guesses positional arguments from their meaning rather than their position

exercises.title: Match the arguments
hints: Match the arguments to the parameter list from left to right.
Mira becomes name; Scout becomes role.
The returned string is Mira: Scout.

exercises.title: Complete the signature
exercises.prompt: Complete the function signature so the body can multiply `price` by `quantity`.
exercises.reference_solution:
def total(price, quantity):
    return price * quantity
hints: The body uses two separate inputs.
Both names used as required inputs should appear inside the parentheses of the definition.

exercises.title: Argument order changes the result
hints: Do not reorder the values by meaning; use their call positions.
B is the first argument, so it becomes first. A becomes second.

exercises.title: Fix the call site
exercises.prompt: The function is correct, but the call passes the values in the wrong order. Repair only the call so the program prints `Mira: Scout`.
hints: Read the parameter order in the definition first.
The first argument must be the character name; the second must be the role.

exercises.title: Carry capacity
exercises.prompt: Write `carry_capacity(base_slots, bonus_slots)` that returns the sum of its two inputs. Both parameters must affect the result. Negative bonus values should reduce the total normally.
exercises.reference_solution:
def carry_capacity(base_slots, bonus_slots):
    return base_slots + bonus_slots
hints: The function needs only one arithmetic expression.
Use both parameter names rather than a fixed number.

exercises.title: Dispatch Status
exercises.prompt: Write `dispatch_status(party, supplies, warning_active)`. Return `"Denied"` if a warning is active OR the party is empty. Otherwise return `"Ready"` when there are at least two supply items for each party member. Return `"Review"` for the remaining cases. Use all three parameters; do not hardcode one sample party size.
hints: Handle denial first: either an active warning or an empty party is enough.
If departure is not denied, compare the supply count with two times the party count.
Use `if warning_active or len(party) == 0`, then an `elif` comparing `len(supplies)` with `len(party) * 2`, then `else`.
exercises.success_message: Dispatch status responds correctly to empty parties, warnings, exact supply boundaries, and undersupply.
